findings.title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, so every AssignmentSource shares the same timestamp
findings.body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass default, which Python evaluates a single time when the class body executes (i.e. at module import). Every `AssignmentSource` created for the lifetime of the process therefore carries the process-start timestamp rather than the time the assignment was queued, making the field useless for debugging/ordering and misleading to anyone who later relies on it (e.g. to expire stale sources). Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead. As a secondary effect, evaluating `timezone.now()` in the class body touches Django settings (`USE_TZ`) at import time of a module that is imported by `sentry/models/groupassignee.py`.

findings.title: AssignmentSource round-trip through Celery kwargs corrupts the `queued` type and silently drops the source on any mismatch
findings.body: `to_dict()` (via `asdict`) emits a raw `datetime` for `queued`, and that dict is passed as a Celery task kwarg in `sync_group_assignee_outbound`. With the JSON task serializer the datetime is encoded as an ISO string and is never decoded back, so `from_dict` reconstructs an instance whose `queued` field is a `str` even though it is annotated `datetime` (and with a stricter serializer the publish would fail outright, breaking assignee sync). `from_dict` performs no type validation and only catches `ValueError`/`TypeError`, returning `None` without logging, which means any future schema drift (renamed/extra key) silently yields no assignment source and re-enables the sync loop this PR is meant to fix. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. isoformat string) and log when parsing fails.

findings.title: Abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` was not updated for the new `assignment_source` kwarg that the task now passes
findings.body: `sync_assignee_outbound` in `src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py` now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, but the abstract declaration here still only lists `external_issue, user, assign, **kwargs`. The new keyword is only tolerated because concrete implementations happen to declare `**kwargs`; any implementation (current or third-party/plugin shim) that does not will raise `TypeError`, which the `@retry` decorator will retry and then drop, silently disabling outbound assignee sync for that provider. The contract should declare `assignment_source` explicitly so implementers know it exists.

findings.title: `assignment_source` added to abstract `sync_status_outbound` but never passed or implemented
findings.body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` before `**kwargs`, yet no call site (e.g. `sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_status_outbound.py`) passes it and no concrete integration implementation declares it. The result is a parameter in the published contract that is positionally inconsistent with subclass signatures (`(external_issue, is_resolved, project_id, **kwargs)`), so a positional call would bind the value to the wrong argument in subclasses, and keyword calls are silently swallowed into `**kwargs`. Either wire status sync through the same loop-breaking check or drop the parameter until it is implemented.

findings.title: `should_sync` is called with the new argument positionally, breaking any one-argument override
findings.body: `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` passes the new source positionally. Only `IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` and `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` were widened in this PR; any installation class that overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-argument signature will now raise `TypeError` inside a retried task, disabling assignee sync for that provider. Passing it as a keyword (and/or defaulting it) would at least make such breakage explicit and greppable.

findings.title: No test covers the task-level dict round trip, and `test_to_dict` cannot detect the frozen `queued` default
findings.body: `assert result.get("queued") is not None` always passes because `queued` has a class-level default, so the test gives no coverage of the timestamp actually reflecting when the source was created, nor of the dict surviving a serialize/deserialize cycle (`to_dict()` -> Celery JSON -> `from_dict()`), which is the path that actually breaks the loop. Tests using `self.tasks()` run tasks eagerly and skip kwarg serialization, so the datetime handling is untested end to end. Add a test that feeds `to_dict()` output through JSON encode/decode into `from_dict` and asserts the resulting `integration_id`/`queued` types, plus a deassign-with-matching-source case mirroring the new assign test.
